idiom_name: hand-written subclass with override (@testable import, non-final members)
implementation_notes: Swift supports the classic form directly: a test-only subclass with an override method (the compiler checks that it actually overrides), and @testable import gives the test target the extra access needed to subclass non-final internal and public classes and override their non-final members - SE-0117 keeps exactly that behaviour. It fails where the ecosystem pushes: final classes and members cannot be subclassed, a type from another module must be open (with open members), and structs and enums - the default choice for models - have no inheritance at all. The idiomatic alternative is protocol-oriented dependency injection; use the subclass only where the boundary type is concrete and unchangeable.
pitfalls: final on the class or the method is the standard Swift optimization and removes the seam; with @testable, internal/public members can be overridden only while they stay non-final.
A class imported from another module can only be subclassed if it is open and its members are open too; public alone allows use but not overriding.
Structs and enums cannot be subclassed at all, so the pattern is unavailable for the value types Swift culture favours - wrap the boundary in a protocol there.
